correctness.rationale: Dyadic \(\varphi(n)\) and the unit equation force dyadic \(\varphi(\sigma(n))\). The Gauss–Wantzel factorization is exhaustive. Any Fermat prime \(F_j\) with \(j\ge2\) introduces a divisor \(F_j+1\mid\sigma(n)\) whose totient has an odd factor, via the odd-exponent multiplicative-order obstruction. The remaining supports \(2^a3^\varepsilon5^\delta\) are exhausted explicitly; the pure dyadic and \(3\)-dyadic rays reduce to \(\varphi(2^{a+1}-1)=2^a\), whose five solutions follow from the Fermat-product identity and the known prime factor \(641\mid F_5\). The sufficiency and all boundaries including \(n=1\), odd candidates, and \(a=1\) are accounted for.

value.rationale: The exact 2006 A116083 problem conjectures only ten solutions. The Gauss–Wantzel class \(\varphi(n)=2^k\) is a canonical unbounded arithmetic and geometric family containing all ten. The theorem settles the complete equation on that entire class without assumptions about possible undiscovered Fermat primes, and proves that any future additional solution must have an odd prime divisor of its totient. This is a substantive global structural reduction rather than a finite list or an arbitrary parameter slice.
